messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: standard vector type
parts:
At some point in the future, we'll add a standard_vector data type.
For now, you can use the following encoding in terms of unit
vectors:

parameters {
unit_vector[K] x_raw; // mean(x_raw) = 0; var(x_raw) = 1 / K
}
transformed parameters {
vector[K] x;
x <- sqrt(K) * x_raw; // mean(x) = 0; var(x) = 1
}

The Jacobian is a constant, so we can ignore it and work with x.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] standard vector type [not]
parts:
Sorry, that's not going to work, because the unit_vector
isn't standardized to have mean(x_raw) = 0, so that means
there's no guarantee that var(x_raw) = 1 / K, just because
sum(x_raw^2) = 1. It would require:

x <- (x_raw - mean(x_raw)) / sd(x_raw);

which can take an unconstrained x_raw, but has a non-trivial Jacobian.

Back to the drawing board.

- Bob

What is the use case here? Standardization could be useful for data, but I have a harder time thinking of when it would be useful for a parameter. And if it were used for a parameter, I have a harder time thinking of a case where we would need to do more than use a prior whose mean is zero.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] standard vector type [not]
parts:
On 6/24/13 1:40 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> What is the use case here? Standardization could be useful for data, but I have a harder time thinking of when it would
> be useful for a parameter. And if it were used for a parameter, I have a harder time thinking of a case where we would
> need to do more than use a prior whose mean is zero.

I'll cite chapter and verse, though it's not clear it'll be very
useful :-)

Gelman and Hill, Chapter 14, Section 14.3, subsection "An ideal-point model for Supreme
Court voting", says, with respect to identification,

We can resolve both these indeterminancies by constraining
the alpha[j]'s to have mean 0 and standard deviation 1

and then finishes the sentence with,

or, in a multilevel context, by giving the alpha[j] a N(0,1) distribution.

For the simple IRT models in the previous subsection, they
suggest centering w/o scale standardization.

Of course, if we only need to use the transformed parameter on the right side
of later statements, then we can just use

y <- (y_raw - mean(y_raw)) / sd(y_raw)

But again, I'm not sure what the implications are for the prior -- it's a pretty
involved set of derivatives in the Jacobian.

- Bob

P.S. Copy-editing cap on. I'd suggest sticking to one
of "the alpha", "the alpha[j]", or "the alpha[j]s" (no possessive)
throughout.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] standard vector type [not]
parts:
On Tuesday, June 25, 2013 11:27:33 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
On 6/24/13 1:40 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> What is the use case here? Standardization could be useful for data, but I have a harder time thinking of when it would
> be useful for a parameter. And if it were used for a parameter, I have a harder time thinking of a case where we would
> need to do more than use a prior whose mean is zero.

I'll cite chapter and verse, though it's not clear it'll be very
useful :-)

Gelman and Hill, Chapter 14, Section 14.3, subsection "An ideal-point model for Supreme
Court voting", says, with respect to identification,

   We can resolve both these indeterminancies by constraining
   the alpha[j]'s to have mean 0 and standard deviation 1
 

and then finishes the sentence with,

   or, in a multilevel context, by giving the alpha[j] a N(0,1) distribution.

My understanding is that, in a unidimensional model, the posterior distribution will be curved everywhere as long as the prior distribution on the ideal points has a fixed mean and standard deviation. In other words, in that case, we don't need a variable type that has mean zero and unit standard deviation, we just need a iid normal(0,1) prior on a plain vector[N]. There is still an indeterminacy with the sign in the sense that you can multiply the ideal points by -1 and the coefficients by -1 and get the same predictions for the outcomes, but that can be overcome by constraining some ideal point to be positive.

The multidimensional case is harder. Again, you can curve the posterior with a multi_normal(zeros, Sigma) prior where Sigma is a correlation matrix, and again you have the small problem that you can multiply by -1. The bigger problem is that you can do a symmetric permutation of the rows and columns of Sigma and the same permutation of the columns of the ideal points and get the same predictions for the outcomes. In this case, you really want some sort of an ordering constraint on some of the coefficients.

Ben
